newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China's poor seek new life off the land.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China's poor seek new life off the land.

text.p: When World Bank officials hiked into mountain hamlets in southwestern China a few years ago to set up a relief project, they asked poor villagers what they needed most to improve life on the farm.
The answer from peasants like Luo Daoyou, struggling to wrest a living from the rugged and remote terrain, was simple -- jobs off the farms.
That desire to escape the impoverished soil and hardship led to a pioneering bank project to encourage poor villagers to lay down their hoes and seek their fortunes in cities and towns.
"You put anyone in those villages, you're going to be poor," said Alan Piazza, task manager of the bank's Southwest Poverty Reduction Project in China.

Tens of millions of Chinese living below the poverty line are increasingly concentrated in mountainous areas -- such as the southwestern region of Guangxi -- where farming is difficult and industry nearly impossible to establish, Piazza said.
Luo Daoyou comes from Haokun, a hamlet set among Guangxi's jade-green hills and soaring limestone peaks that mask his poverty.
Luo can grow only enough food in the exhausted red soil of his tiny plot to feed his family of seven for six months of the year.
"It's not enough," he says. "The land is so rocky."
Luo's family survives on government grain rations and by seeking work elsewhere -- a solution the World Bank is hoping to systematise.
"You just don't have the resource base to be self-sufficient in agriculture," Piazza told reporters on a recent trip to project sites in Guangxi.
FROM FARMS TO FACTORIES
In one of its biggest projects in China, the World Bank plans to spend $247 million over six years on poverty relief in Guangxi, Yunnan and Guizhou, some of the worst-off regions and provinces.

Feng Qiang, a poverty official under the State Council, or cabinet, said the money and counterpart funding from Beijing, would be used in part to provide loans to help farmers raise livestock and to build schools and clinics.

Some of the funds have already gone to support an employment plan that since 1995 has found jobs for 70,000 poor villagers in local towns or cities as far away as Shenzhen, a glittering metropolis just over the border from Hong Kong, Feng said.

Piazza said the programme met initial resistance from Chinese officials who were more keen on setting up small-scale enterprises in the country. They were wary about the prospect of rural labourers flooding into already crowded cities.
"They initially wanted a much larger TVE (township and village enterprise) component," Piazza said. "But there's just not any industry that can be competitive in these areas."

He said the bank had lobbied hard for the labour mobility plan, arguing it would allow poor peasants to send money back home, where it could be invested in business sidelines such as raising livestock.
"The principle objective is to establish and test a new model of poverty reduction in China," Piazza said. "If the farmers aren't interested, it won't work."
SAFE, RELIABLE, GUARANTEED
In Guangxi's Lingyun county -- one of the poorest areas of a poor region -- the labour mobility programme has found jobs for more than 3,000 farmers since late 1995, local officials said.

A local joint venture company set up by the World Bank and local government helps would-be workers find jobs in other areas and gives them low-interest loans to cover travel and one month's living expenses away from home.
The poorest farmers, with annual incomes under the official poverty line of 530 yuan ($64), are given priority for jobs from which they can often send home as much as 2,000 yuan a year.
Advertisements for the programme are posted throughout the county lauding the rewards of working off-farm as "Reliable. Safe. Guaranteed".
Piazza said factory life was better than conditions on many farms, where infant mortality could reach as high as 20 percent and diarrhoea and respiratory illness were common killers.
Less than 10 percent of those sent to work in other areas request a change of assignment and even fewer end up leaving the programme to return home.
To help ex-farmers cope with life in the big city, the company distributes a cartoon book filled with helpful hints -- ranging from how to address a letter to what to do if mugged.
Piazza said he hoped the plan would open the way to getting poor farming families out of the fields for good.
"That was never our objective, to resettle people, but if it happens, so much the better."
